verses.commentary: Joel son of Pethuel receives divine word. No date given, making the message timeless. The prophet's name means 'Yahweh is God,' a fitting declaration for a book about divine sovereignty over nature and history.

Elders and inhabitants summoned to hear. Unprecedented disaster demands unprecedented attention. The rhetorical question challenges collective memory. Nothing in ancestral experience compares to what has happened.
Four generations commanded to transmit the story. Tell children, grandchildren, great grandchildren. Memory becomes obligation. What God does, his people must remember and recount.
Four stages of locusts: swarming, great, young, other. Whether four literal species or poetic amplification, the effect is total devastation. What one wave misses, the next consumes. Nothing escapes.
Drunkards must wake and weep. The numbing comfort of wine is snatched away. Those most dependent on pleasure face its sudden absence. Crisis strips away diversions.
The locust plague described as a nation invading. Countless as an army, fierce as lions. Agricultural disaster becomes military imagery. Nature itself wages war.
Vines and fig trees ruined. Bark stripped, branches white. The covenant blessings of vine and fig (Micah 4:4) reversed. Prosperity becomes desolation. The garden becomes wasteland.
The land should mourn like a virgin for her dead betrothed. Deep, inconsolable grief. The relationship with the land mirrors spousal intimacy. Loss is personal, not merely economic.
Temple worship disrupted. No grain or drink offerings possible. Priests mourn because they cannot perform their sacred duties. When agriculture fails, worship fails. Heaven and earth are connected.
Fields ruined, ground mourns (Hebrew 'abel' means both mourning and dried up). Grain, wine, oil: the triad of covenant blessing destroyed. The land itself grieves.
Farmers despair, vinedressers wail. Those who work the land feel its devastation most acutely. Wheat and barley, staples of survival, gone. The harvest that sustains life vanishes.
Seven trees listed: vine, fig, pomegranate, palm, apple, all field trees. Complete botanical devastation. Joy withers with the vegetation. Human emotion mirrors natural conditions.
Priests commanded to don sackcloth and lament. All night vigil in mourning garments. Religious leaders must embody the grief. Ministry requires entering the darkness of the moment.
Sacred assembly declared. Fast proclaimed. Gather elders and all people at the Lord's house. Corporate crisis demands corporate response. Individual piety cannot substitute for communal repentance.

Alas (ahah), an untranslatable groan. The day of the Lord arrives as destruction (shod) from the Almighty (Shaddai). Wordplay in Hebrew: shod from Shaddai. Devastation comes from the All Sufficient One.
Food cut off before watching eyes. Joy removed from God's house. The present tense intensifies the experience. Not past disaster but ongoing deprivation. Starvation unfolds in real time.
Seeds shrivel beneath dry soil. Granaries ruined, grain dried up. Agricultural infrastructure collapses. Even stored provisions fail. The future harvest and past surplus both destroyed.
Animals suffer too. Cattle groan, herds mill aimlessly without pasture. Sheep suffer. Creation groans under the curse (Romans 8:22). Innocent creatures share in judgment's effects.

The prophet cries directly to God. Fire has consumed pastures, flames burned trees. Whether literal fire or metaphor for drought, the wilderness itself is destroyed. Even untended nature offers no refuge.
Wild animals pant for God (or toward God). Streams dry up. Creation itself reaches for its Creator in distress. The whole earth groans for divine intervention. Nature prays.
